sample_query.user_prompt:
This person is a 24-year-old barista in London Zone 2 working zero-hours at a chain cafe, who wants any minimum wage rise to include a London weighting, guaranteed minimum weekly hours, a ban on unpaid 'trial' shifts, and stronger HMRC enforcement so on-call and pre-opening prep time is counted and paid. Last month I worked a five-hour unpaid trial and spent 30 minutes setting up before three shifts that never made it onto my timesheet. I care most that on-call time is paid, because last week I had to stay within 15 minutes of the store for four hours and never got called in—or paid. I even turned down a £50 evening temp shift to stay within 15 minutes of the cafe on-call, and ended up unpaid. If on-call hours aren’t legally paid, a higher minimum wage won’t stop me losing income to unpaid dead time.

They are reviewing opinion statements on the question: "Should we raise the minimum wage in the UK?"

OPINION STATEMENT:
Yes, we should raise the minimum wage.
We have recently seen that the UK is suffering from a cost of living crisis and that inflation is at a staggering rate. We have also seen that wages are stagnating, not rising at the same rate that the cost of living is rising, making it harder for people to provide for themselves. Therefore, the minimum wage should be raised to reflect this.
There is a problem with income disparity in the UK today. The minimum wage should be raised to ensure that the gap is closed.

They consider how the opinion statement would translate into real-world policy actions. A candidate proposal is given below:

POLICY PROPOSAL:
Minimum Wage Indexation and Glidepath Order: Set a statutory target for the National Living Wage to reach 66% of median hourly pay by 2030, with annual uprating each April by the lower of CPI+1% or the increase needed to stay on the glidepath; include an automatic pause trigger if unemployment in low-wage sectors rises by more than 0.5 percentage points over two consecutive quarters, subject to Low Pay Commission review; retain a distinct apprentice rate for two years; complement the policy by increasing Universal Credit work allowances by 10% and cutting the taper by 2 percentage points to reduce in-work poverty; tradeoffs include slower wage gains during high inflation and operational complexity of the triggers.

After thinking carefully from their own point of view, they answer a yes/no question.
Question: Does the intention of the policy proposal support/is compatible with the principles and beliefs described in the opinion statement?

prompt_construction:
def prompt_fn(*, rater:str, policy:str, case:str, scenario_params:dict, instruct_tuned:bool=False) -> list[str]:
    base_context = (
        f"{rater}\n\n"
        f"They are reviewing opinion statements on the question: \"{scenario_params['question']}\"\n\n"
        f"OPINION STATEMENT:\n{policy}\n\n"
        f"They consider how the opinion statement would translate into real-world policy actions. A candidate proposal is given below:\n\n"
        f"POLICY PROPOSAL:\n{case}\n\n"
        "After thinking carefully from their own point of view, they answer a yes/no question.\n"
    )

    prompt1 = (
        base_context +
        "Question: Does the intention of the policy proposal support/is compatible with the principles and beliefs described in the opinion statement?"
    )

    prompt2 = (
        base_context +
        "Question: Does the intention of the policy proposal contradict/stand in opposition to the principles and beliefs described in the opinion statement?"
    )

    if instruct_tuned:
        return [prompt1, prompt2]

    prompts = [prompt1, prompt2]
    prompts = [p + "\nAnswer:" for p in prompts]
    return prompts

This person is a county council finance director in North Yorkshire responsible for adult social care budgets, who insists any increase be announced at least 12 months ahead and legally linked to corresponding increases in the Social Care Grant and Public Health Grant, plus flexibility on council tax caps or central top-ups to prevent cuts elsewhere. If rises are unfunded or announced late, I’ll have to raise care home and homecare fee rates mid‑year or risk provider failure and hospital discharge backlogs. My biggest concern is aligning NLW announcements with our April fee‑setting cycle so we can price them into contracts rather than issuing costly in‑year variations. Last winter I had to reopen and vary over 300 homecare and care‑home contracts after a late NLW decision, racking up extra legal/procurement costs and worsening hospital discharge delays.

This person is a 19-year-old apprentice electrician in Greater Manchester paying for tools and bus fare, who wants the lower apprentice rate scrapped after the first six months, mandatory payment of training and college hours at the full rate, and a travel allowance or tool grant funded alongside the wage rise so apprentices can afford to complete. This person is a small-business owner of an eight-person electrical contracting SME in Salford who relies on apprentices, and advocates keeping a distinct apprentice rate with a slower glide path, paired with an apprentice wage credit or employer NIC rebate, and at least a six-month lead time so existing fixed-price contracts are not loss-making. This person is a ride-hailing and delivery driver in Birmingham logged into apps 50 hours a week, who wants the policy to clarify that waiting and queuing time counts as working time, set a guaranteed per-hour floor across multi-app shifts, require algorithmic transparency on pay calculations, and fund HMRC to run proactive audits of platforms. When I asked Uber and Bolt for a pay breakdown, both said the calculations were proprietary, which is why algorithmic transparency and a multi‑app hourly floor are my top priorities. If the hourly floor only applies per app, I’d have to stop multi‑apping to qualify and would end up earning less in off‑peak hours after petrol and insurance.

This person is a public policy head at a UK gig-economy platform, who argues for a sector code allowing per-job pay as long as average earnings meet the minimum over a defined shift window, a clear statutory definition of logged-in versus working time, a 12 to 18 month transition period, and credit against the floor for guaranteed earnings top-ups the platform already provides. This person is a 72-year-old pensioner in rural Pembrokeshire on a fixed income who worries about wage-driven price pass-through on essentials, and favors smaller, predictable annual upratings tied to CPI with a sunset review, alongside temporary support like energy bill rebates if inflation spikes during implementation. This person is a regional operations director for a major supermarket chain in the North West, who seeks a single national rate to reduce payroll complexity, a clear plan to manage pay compression for team leaders, at least six months' notice for price file and supplier renegotiations, and offsets such as temporary business rates relief to avoid pushing up shelf prices. This person is a 27-year-old hotel housekeeper in London working split shifts on the current minimum wage; she wants any rise to include a London-weighted National Living Wage rate, mandatory pay for travel time and cleaning trolley setup between shifts, outlawing unpaid 'turnaround' minutes, stronger HMRC enforcement against wage theft, and coordination with Universal Credit so higher pay is not immediately lost to a steep taper. This person is a small independent cafe owner in Hackney employing 12 staff; he supports a clear multi-year uplift timetable, but insists it be phased with at least 12 months' notice, keep differentiated apprentice and under-21 rates, raise the employer NICs threshold or give a small-firm rebate, clarify that service charges cannot be used to meet the wage floor, and provide temporary business rates relief to avoid cutting hours. While auditing Surrey County Council's adult social care contracts early in his career, he saw minimum wage increases outpace funding settlements and force either service cuts or council tax rises. When his grandmother’s council-funded home care package was cut after a past NLW rise drove up provider rates, he saw firsthand how blunt mandates can backfire on services. If ministers push rapid NLW hikes without extra grant funding, he fears Surrey will either cut care hours again, like his gran’s, or hike the adult social care precept. As a Surrey council taxpayer with his gran still relying on council-funded home care, he fears unfunded NLW hikes will push up his adult social care precept and risk another cut to her hours.

This person is a community organizer in Lincolnshire working with seasonal migrant farm workers who wants the rise enforced through greater GLAA and HMRC budgets, mandatory digital timesheets in workers' languages, limits on the accommodation offset, and joint liability up the supply chain so supermarkets share penalties when labour providers underpay; she cares because she routinely sees piece-rate systems pushing effective pay below the legal minimum. If the wage goes up without a tighter cap on the accommodation offset, I’ve seen caravan charges quietly rise and erase most of the gain.

Temporary policy: A 24‑month “Cost‑of‑Living Escalator” that adjusts the minimum wage quarterly by CPI +0.5% (capped at 2% per quarter), with an automatic sunset and Low Pay Commission review; no regional variation; SMEs receive a partial, time‑limited employer NIC holiday to cushion cash flow; tradeoff: risk of wage‑price feedback and payroll volatility.

Pilot freeze policy: Authorise designated low‑cost local authorities to issue 12‑month minimum‑wage freeze permits to micro‑businesses (<10 employees, turnover <£500k) conditional on no layoffs, a prices freeze on core goods/services, and 40 hours of paid training per worker; affected employees receive a £500 council‑administered heating voucher funded by central government; tradeoff: fairness concerns and patchwork coverage.

National policy: Implement a two-year freeze on the statutory minimum wage while introducing a £400/month universal basic income for all adults, funded by a 1% net-wealth levy above £2 million and a temporary 3% surcharge on incomes over £150,000; conduct an independent review of employment and price effects before resuming minimum-wage increases (tradeoffs: higher public spending, risk of wage stagnation in low-wage sectors).

National policy: Legislate automatic annual uprating of the minimum wage to match CPIH inflation plus a housing-cost component, retaining age bands but narrowing gaps to within 5 percentage points; adjust Universal Credit tapers so a full-time minimum-wage earner can cover basic necessities after housing costs, minimizing benefit cliffs.

National Living Wage Indexation and Youth Parity Act: Peg the National Living Wage to an independent cost-of-living index (CPIH including housing costs) with automatic annual uprating each April, and abolish lower minimum wage rates for 18–20 year-olds over a 24-month phase-in; provide a time-limited National Insurance rebate for small firms to smooth adjustment. Tradeoff: higher payroll costs may raise prices or reduce hiring in some sectors once rebates expire.

Secure Hours and Minimum Income Floor: Require employers using zero-hours or on-call scheduling to offer a contract guaranteeing the worker’s 12-week average hours after 12 weeks, or pay a 25 percent wage premium for shifts confirmed with less than 7 days’ notice; mandate a minimum 3 hours’ pay for any shift canceled after arrival or for required standby periods. Tradeoff: employers may reduce last-minute scheduling flexibility and tightly manage available hours.

National One-Rate Living Wage: Establish a single statutory minimum wage for all workers aged 18+ set at 65% of median hourly pay, with automatic annual uprating by the higher of CPIH inflation or median wage growth; abolish age bands; create a 12-month Small Employer Transition Grant funded by a 2% surtax on personal incomes above £200,000; introduce a temporary Universal Credit earnings disregard (£60/month) to ensure the wage rise does not trigger benefit reductions for low-income households.

Local Living Wage Powers: Authorize combined authorities and devolved administrations to set regional minimum wage supplements up to 20% above the national floor based on local housing and transport cost indices, retain existing age bands during a three-year pilot, and allow hardship waivers for micro-businesses; tradeoff: added compliance complexity and potential cross-border job shifting.

National policy: Raise the National Living Wage to 66% of median hourly pay by April 2027 (to ~£12.50 in 2026 and ~£13.20 in 2027), abolish remaining age bands down to 18, and thereafter index it annually to the higher of CPIH inflation or median wage growth; no small-firm exemptions; HMRC enforcement and penalties doubled to ensure compliance. Tradeoff: near-term price pass-through and wage compression risks for lower-margin sectors.

National policy: Implement a two-tier minimum wage for 24 months to manage cost pressures—freeze the current rate for micro-firms (fewer than 10 employees) while requiring large employers (250+ employees) to raise their firm-wide minimum to £12.80 immediately, with a 5% London premium; medium firms phase to the higher rate over 18 months. Government provides targeted relief to micro-firms via business rates rebates and enforces anti-avoidance rules to prevent artificial firm-splitting. Tradeoff: uneven pay by employer size and incentives to game thresholds.

Government Wage Credit Uplift: From April next year, set the statutory National Living Wage equal to the independent UK Living Wage benchmark nationwide; to limit price pass-through, HM Treasury pays a declining wage credit to employers covering 50% of the incremental hourly cost in year 1, 30% in year 2, and 10% in year 3; participating firms must cap price rises on a defined essentials basket to CPI for 12 months and suspend dividends and share buybacks while subsidised; enforced by HMRC with penalties and clawbacks. Tradeoffs: high fiscal outlay and compliance burden; a temporary surcharge on large corporate profits to fund credits may dampen investment.

National Staircase Minimum Wage Plan: Raise the National Living Wage on a published three-year schedule (CPI + 1% annually, with a 4-8% band) until it reaches two-thirds of median hourly pay by 2029; pair with a Small Employer Transition Package (temporary 2 percentage point employer NIC reduction for wages at or below the new NLW, tapering over two years) and an Inclusive Hiring Credit of £1 per hour for up to 24 months for employees with certified learning disabilities or recent criminal records; Low Pay Commission reviews annually and can adjust within the band if unemployment spikes. Tradeoffs: slower relief for workers; fiscal and administrative costs.

Local policy: Introduce a City Living Wage of £14.00 in Greater London and £13.00 in Core Cities (Manchester, Birmingham, Leeds, Liverpool, Newcastle), pegged to local housing cost indices and updated annually by CPI plus rent inflation; 3-year phase-in; small employers (under 50 staff) receive a temporary employer NIC rebate covering 50% of the incremental wage bill; tradeoff: regional differentials may complicate payroll and create border effects.

National policy: Raise the National Living Wage to £12.50 in April 2026, rising to £15.00 by April 2028; abolish lower age bands so all workers 18+ receive the same rate; index thereafter to 66% of median hourly pay; justification: align wages with cost of living so full-time work covers rent, council tax, utilities and food; tradeoff: higher labour costs may raise prices and pressure jobs in low-margin sectors, mitigated by a 24-month phase-in for firms with fewer than 20 employees.

Company-focused, opt-in scheme: A UK Fair Pricing and Wage Pact for large consumer-facing firms (e.g., supermarkets, hospitality chains) that raise base pay to at least the independently calculated Real Living Wage within 12 months and commit to capping UK gross profit margin growth to CPI+1% for two years in exchange for temporary business rates relief and accelerated capital allowances; requires quarterly publication of UK price and margin data with clawbacks for non-compliance. Tradeoffs: administrative burden and potential investment disincentives for participants.

National policy: Abolish age-based minimum wage rates and the lower apprentice rate within 12 months, establishing a single statutory floor for all workers aged 16+ equal to the adult National Living Wage; provide a £1,000 per new 16–20-year-old hire training grant to SMEs for two years, funded by a 1% surcharge on discretionary bonuses over £100,000 in financial services. Tradeoffs: risk of reduced youth hiring without effective training support; sector-specific levy may face pushback.

Local sectoral phase-in pilot: authorise 10 combined authorities to pilot a sector-specific minimum wage pathway in hospitality and adult social care, with an immediate £1/hour uplift and a phased increase to the national target over 24 months; eligibility for the phase-in requires employers to convert zero-hours staff to guaranteed-hours contracts and provide accredited training; councils issue £20/month healthy food and activity cards to affected workers during the phase-in; sunset after three years with an independent evaluation, while firms that do not opt in must pay the full national minimum immediately. Tradeoffs: uneven treatment across regions and sectors; administrative burden for councils and SMEs.

National 'Work More, Keep More' package: raise the National Living Wage to £12.50 within 12 months and index it to CPI+0.5; cut the Universal Credit taper from 55% to 45% and raise work allowances so extra hours translate into higher take-home pay; fund the taper change and enforcement from projected reductions in out-of-work and in-work benefit spending as earnings rise, with no increases in taxation; provide NHS-backed £30/month Healthy Living vouchers for minimum-wage workers redeemable on healthy food and active hobbies. Tradeoffs: fiscal risk if savings are slower than expected; administrative complexity of voucher delivery.

Set a single National Living Wage for all workers aged 18+ at the independently calculated Real Living Wage, with automatic annual uprating tied to CPI and median private rent growth; abolish lower youth rates; 18-month phase-in with targeted grants and low-interest loans to small firms to adapt; tradeoff: higher payroll costs in youth-heavy sectors may raise prices or reduce entry-level hours.

Increase the adult National Living Wage (21+) by 12% next April while retaining age bands (18–20 paid at 90% of the adult rate, apprentices on a protected rate); simultaneously cut the Universal Credit taper from 55% to 45% and provide a one-year employer National Insurance rebate for firms with fewer than 50 staff to preserve hiring; tradeoff: higher fiscal cost and added administrative complexity.

National policy: Introduce a Secure Hours Wage package: increase the statutory minimum by 50p/hour in year one, require a 20% pay premium for any shift given with less than 14 days' notice or on zero-hours contracts, and grant a right to a contract reflecting average hours after 12 weeks; tradeoff: less scheduling flexibility for employers but more predictable incomes.

National policy: Raise the National Living Wage to 66% of median hourly pay, apply one rate from age 18+, and index it annually to CPIH plus private rent; phase in over 24 months with a temporary National Insurance rebate for small employers; tradeoff: higher labour costs may raise prices or reduce hours during the transition.

Set a single national living wage of £13/hour immediately, rising to at least 60% of median earnings by 2027 with automatic indexation to CPI inflation or median earnings growth (whichever is higher); ban unpaid trial shifts and require firms with 250+ employees to publish pay distributions to discourage the minimum from becoming the de facto maximum; no new taxes or subsidies.

Temporarily freeze the statutory minimum wage for microbusinesses (fewer than 10 employees) for 24 months, while introducing a government wage top-up of up to £2/hour paid directly to workers via Universal Credit with a lower taper and higher work allowance; cap eligibility to sectors facing acute energy or rent cost shocks and sunset the subsidy after two years to protect jobs while improving take-home pay without raising employer costs.

National (sectoral): Mandate a 15% wage uplift for workers in social care, hospitality, and food retail, paired with an 18‑month CMA‑enforced fair‑pricing code that limits net margin expansion above the 2019–2023 average and requires cost‑justified price increases; provide targeted transition grants to small care providers to prevent service closures. Tradeoffs: compliance burdens and potential dampening of investment.

SME‑specific (time‑limited freeze with worker protection): Allow micro‑businesses (≤10 employees and ≤£500k turnover) to freeze wages at the current minimum for up to 24 months if they publicly register, disclose accounts, and maintain headcount, while workers receive a government hourly top‑up to the new national rate via PAYE; fund the top‑up with a temporary 0.5% VAT uplift on luxury goods. Tradeoffs: fiscal cost, administrative complexity, and uneven competition between firms.

12‑month minimum wage freeze paired with enhanced in‑work support: Freeze the National Minimum Wage for one year while increasing Universal Credit work allowances, introducing a refundable low‑wage earnings supplement paid monthly, and expanding help with energy/rent for low‑income workers; automatically revert to CPI indexation the following year and sunset the supplement once real pay recovers; tradeoff: shifts burden to taxpayers and may weaken employer incentives to raise pay.

National CPI indexation with small-business offset and review: Legislate automatic annual uprating of the National Minimum Wage each April by CPI inflation, alongside a temporary National Insurance rebate covering 50% of the incremental wage bill for firms with fewer than 50 employees (capped per firm), with the Low Pay Commission required to certify labour market conditions each year or trigger a 6‑month pause if GDP contracts for two consecutive quarters; tradeoff: fiscal cost and potential price pass‑through.

Local living wage powers tied to cost-of-living: Authorise devolved administrations and local councils to set local minimum wages up to 20% above the national floor using a formula linked to local housing and transport costs, backed by a one-year hardship grant for very small employers to adapt, with a statutory ban on setting rates below the national NLW; tradeoff: improves alignment with local prices but creates patchwork compliance costs and risks shifting jobs across borders.

Statutory phased NLW escalator with inclusion safeguards: Legislate semiannual minimum wage increases on a published path to 66% of median earnings over four years, paired with a time-limited small business employer NICs rebate on the first slice of additional wage costs and a Wage Inclusion Credit that subsidises wages for hires of people with learning disabilities or criminal records paid at or above the new floor; include an automatic pause if employment rates for these groups fall beyond set thresholds; tradeoff: adds fiscal cost and complexity, and pause triggers may delay pay gains.

National policy: Introduce a Statutory Living Wage pegged to the Minimum Income Standard, phased in over three years; pair with capped annual rent increases at CPI for three years and an Ofgem-administered energy price cap on basic tariffs; finance enforcement and transition with a 2% surtax on incomes above £150,000 and a temporary windfall levy on excess energy profits; provide small-business transition grants.

National policy: Phase the minimum wage to 60% of median earnings by 2028, with an automatic CPI+0.5% indexation thereafter and a pause trigger if youth unemployment exceeds 12%; offer employer National Insurance rebates and wage subsidies for hiring workers with learning difficulties, ex‑offenders, and the long‑term unemployed; include a time‑limited reduced rate for apprentices and a review of sectoral impacts each year.

National Real Living Wage Act: Raise the National Living Wage to £12.50 for all workers 18+ in April, then to £13.50 the following April; index thereafter to the higher of CPI or 60% of median hourly pay. Provide a 24‑month small business payroll credit worth 60p/hour on the first 20 employees to ease transition. Maintain or increase in‑work benefits (e.g., Universal Credit work allowances) so no household receives a net cut. Fund the policy via a 1% surcharge on corporate profits above £10m and a 2p increase on the top income tax rate above £150k. Tradeoff: higher labour costs may pass through to prices; the payroll credit and phasing mitigate short‑term impacts.

Automatic Escalator with Emergency Brake: Implement an annual minimum wage increase equal to CPI inflation plus 0.5%, bounded to keep the floor between 55% and 66% of median hourly pay. Allow the Low Pay Commission to pause up to half of a scheduled increase for one year if unemployment rises by 1.5 percentage points or GDP falls by 2% over two consecutive quarters. Tradeoff: the brake tempers income gains during downturns but aims to limit layoffs and sharp price pass‑through.

Regional, phased minimum wage indexation with small-business offsets: Set regional minimum wages at 55–60% of each region’s median wage, with three-year phased increases and automatic annual indexation to CPI and productivity. Include an off-ramp that pauses increases if regional unemployment rises by 1.5 percentage points over two consecutive quarters. Offset costs via a National Insurance rebate on the first £2,000 of wage rises per small firm and a time-limited Low Pay Transition Fund for training. Tradeoff: complexity and uneven wage floors across regions.

National Living Wage and Secure Hours Act: Raise the National Living Wage to £12.50 in April 2026 and to 60% of median earnings by 2028, then index annually to CPI or median-wage growth (whichever is lower). Pair with a ban on default zero-hours contracts by requiring worker opt-in and a guaranteed floor of 16 hours/week (or the 12-week average, if higher), plus two-week predictive scheduling and premium pay for late changes. Fund HMRC enforcement and penalties for non-compliance. Tradeoff: higher labour costs could reduce overtime availability and accelerate automation in low-margin sectors.

Impose a 12-month national minimum wage freeze paired with a 12-month statutory freeze on regulated household energy tariffs and a nationwide cap on residential rent increases at 0%, followed by a scheduled 15% catch-up rise in the minimum wage over the subsequent 18 months; fund local enforcement with a temporary 2% surcharge on top-decile earners; tradeoff: delayed wage gains for workers and potential market distortions from price freezes.

Raise the UK National Living Wage to a 'Basket-Based Living Wage' pegged to rent, energy, and a basic food basket, phased in quarterly over 36 months; simultaneously cap annual increases in residential rents and regulated household energy tariffs at 2% during the phase-in; create a time-limited SME Wage Transition Fund financed by a 3% temporary surtax on incomes above £200k and a windfall levy on retail energy suppliers to help small firms meet higher payroll; tradeoff: risks of supply constraints from price caps and administrative complexity.

Local policy pilot: Empower Greater London, Greater Manchester, and West Midlands to set a local minimum wage up to 15% above the national rate, indexed to local CPIH and median rents; provide a 24‑month small‑business rebate covering 50% of the incremental wage cost up to a capped amount, with an independent evaluation on employment, prices, and business survival before wider rollout.

National policy: Implement a 5% increase to the National Living Wage this year alongside a 'Keep More of What You Earn' reform—cut the Universal Credit taper to 45% and raise Work Allowances—funded from forecast reductions in unemployment benefit outlays and administrative savings (no tax rises); issue a 12‑month Healthy Life Card to minimum-wage workers for discounts on fresh food and active hobbies; include an automatic fiscal review clause if projected savings underperform.

Implement an immediate £1.50/hour NLW increase paired with a two-year Wage Uplift Credit for SMEs (<250 employees) that reimburses 50% of the incremental wage cost and funds productivity upgrades and training, financed by a temporary 1% corporation tax surcharge on large firms and an employer NICs rebate for SMEs; eligibility requires open-book verification and a price-growth covenant benchmarked to CPI+1 during the support period.

Adopt a statutory regional living wage formula: raise the National Living Wage to 66% of median pay by 2028 with three tiers (London, high-cost city regions, rest of UK), and automatically uprate annually by a formula tied to regional CPIH and median wage growth with guardrails that pause increases if core inflation exceeds 3.5% or unemployment rises by 0.5 percentage points over two consecutive quarters; an independent impact review must precede each uprating.
